title: Permission to Run
subtitle: Across every store.
description: How clear authority, complementary roles and patience carry a good idea across a dealership group.
dek: A customer can be ready while the organization is still deciding. The ownership work is to give people clear authority, connect their roles and hold the standard through the handoff.
glance: A willing customer reaches a stalled handoff.
In the hypothetical example below, sales, the desk and finance each need the next step to be clear.
Individual capability needs a connected process.
An experienced person can move one deal. Clear roles help the work continue when that person steps away.
Permission, people and patience reinforce one another.
Authority needs boundaries. Different strengths need useful connections. A new routine needs time to be learned.
Judge what carries across stores and shifts.
Watch whether the next person can keep the same customer promise without rebuilding the decision.

ownership.title: The customer sees one business. The work crosses several desks.
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical Friday close at a dealership. The customer has chosen a vehicle. Sales is waiting on a trade decision, the desk is working through an exception, and finance needs a complete handoff. Each person is doing a part of the job. The customer is still waiting.

The useful ownership question is where the work has lost its next owner. Clear authority gives someone room to move. Complementary roles make that judgment useful to the next person. Patience lets the group learn the routine and correct it through actual use.

rail: A hypothetical dealership example makes the operating question visible.
Sales, the desk, finance and delivery each carry a part of it.
A useful routine should be understandable beyond the person who introduced it.
The scenarios are illustrative. The questions are designed for a group with more than one location.

situation.title: The handoff before the close
paragraphs: In that Friday example, the sales associate can explain what the customer wants, but needs a clear route for the exception. The desk needs to know what has already been agreed. Finance needs the same information in a form it can use. Delivery needs to know which promises still require follow-through.

The pause reveals how the roles connect. A decision can be sensible at one desk and incomplete for the next. Ownership can follow the work from the first commitment to the final handoff and see where responsibility becomes uncertain.

context.title: Permission needs enough structure to travel
paragraphs: A capable store leader often carries context that other people cannot see: which exceptions need escalation, where another department is stretched, and which customer commitments require care. Giving that leader room can help the store move. Making the reasoning visible gives the rest of the organization something it can learn.

Across a group, the practical distinction is between a routine that depends on one person’s memory and one whose purpose and boundaries another person can explain. The owner can test that distinction by listening to how people describe the same handoff at different locations.
cards: The decision has a clear owner.
People understand what they can decide, where the limits sit and who handles an exception.
The next person receives the reason.
A handoff carries the customer’s need, the commitment already made and what remains open.

lens.title: The conditions around the work matter
paragraphs: The process needs a purpose people can explain, authority they can use and connections that support the next step. Those conditions make individual judgment more useful to the group.
For ownership, the revealing moment is often the handoff: does the next person inherit a clear job, or have to reconstruct the conversation?

progress.title: What a better close would show
paragraphs: In a revised version of the same hypothetical situation, the associate knows the exception route before reaching the desk. The desk makes the decision within agreed authority. Finance receives the complete context. The delivery team can explain the customer’s remaining commitments.

What to look for is fewer repeated explanations, a clear next owner and promises that remain intact through the change in personnel. A completed deal is one result to examine. How the store completed it tells ownership more about what can be repeated.
That is where the original idea becomes useful across locations. People need to understand why the handoff works well enough to preserve its purpose in a different store.

parts: The owner defines the purpose, the standards that stay fixed and the authority available to pursue them. People can act with a clear understanding of what they are carrying.
The store leader makes judgment visible.
The leader explains how decisions are made and develops others who can carry that reasoning. A routine becomes easier to transfer when its purpose is understood.
Sales and service bring the customer’s need into view.
The people closest to the customer supply context the next department needs. Their observations help the group keep its promise grounded in the actual situation.
The desk and finance connect the decisions.
Each handoff preserves what has been agreed, identifies what remains open and names the person responsible for resolving it.
Staffing, systems, inventory information and training affect whether people can carry out the routine. A good idea needs those connections to hold through a busy day.

second_proof.title: The second proof is the next store
paragraphs: Extend the hypothetical example to another location, with a different mix of experience and a different workload. The original manager is away. The next shift still needs to understand the customer commitment, the authority available and the exception route.

The local details may change. The purpose of the handoff can remain clear. Ownership can watch whether people adapt the routine while preserving the standards behind it, and whether problems reach someone who can resolve them.
That is a stronger test of the operating system than a successful day led by the person who built it. It shows what the organization has learned and where it still relies on individual memory.

framing: Authority has a purpose and a boundary.
People can explain which decisions they own and which need another person’s judgment.
Different strengths need a useful connection.
A strong seller, operator and finance team become more useful to one another when context travels with the work.
A new routine exposes gaps. Specific feedback helps the group correct them while retaining the useful parts.
One strong close is an opening piece of evidence.
The next store, busy period and leadership absence reveal whether the same principles are becoming repeatable.
signals: Watch whether the customer has to repeat the same need when the next department takes over.
The next step has an owner.
Listen for a named person and a clear action when a question moves beyond someone’s authority.
The routine works through an absence.
Observe what continues when the manager who introduced the process is away.
Another store can explain the purpose.
A useful comparison starts with how each location understands the routine, then examines where the work differs.
strategic: Give the work room to move.
Permission becomes useful when people understand the result they are responsible for and the judgment they are trusted to exercise.
Connect the roles around the promise.
The customer commitment is the common thread. Each person should receive enough context to carry it into the next stage.
A change deserves observation through ordinary work and difficult periods. The owner can keep the standard steady while the group improves the routine.
The next person, shift and location provide the evidence. Their ability to continue the work shows how much of the idea the organization now owns.

Examine what arrives at the next desk.

watch: Whether people can explain the authority available to them and the route for an exception.
Whether the customer’s original need reaches the person handling the next stage.
Whether an open commitment has a named owner through a shift change.
Whether another location can explain the purpose of a routine it is adopting.
Whether the work continues when the leader who introduced the routine is away.
Whether a review produces a specific correction people can use on the next handoff.
transcript:
Consider a hypothetical close at one of your dealerships. A customer has chosen a vehicle. Sales is waiting on a trade decision. The desk is handling an exception. Finance needs a complete handoff. Each person is doing a part of the job, and the customer is still waiting.

That pause gives ownership a useful place to look. Who owns the next step? What can that person decide? What information needs to move with the work?

Permission gives people room to exercise judgment inside clear boundaries. The people around them need complementary roles and enough shared context to carry the decision forward. Patience gives the group time to learn the routine and correct it through actual use.

Now carry the same situation to another store. The workload is different. The original manager is away. The next shift still needs to understand the customer commitment, the authority available and the exception route.

That is where an idea begins to show whether the organization has learned it. A completed deal is one result to examine. The way the team completed it shows more about what can be repeated.

As the group moves through its next busy period, follow one exception and one customer promise from the first conversation through delivery. Watch where responsibility stays clear, where context gets lost and what the next person needs to ask again.

The ownership test is whether that next person can carry the same promise forward.
